newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan puts pressure on Israel.
newsitem.headline: Jordan puts pressure on Israel.

text.p: Jordan is likely to use the toughest language since its 1994 peace treaty with Israel when it tells the Jewish state this week that relations hinge on honouring peace accords, officials said on Sunday.

They said Jordan's ambassador to Israel Omar al-Rifai met Netanyahu's political advisor Dore Gold on Sunday to arrange a higher level meeting this week with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to convey the "grave consequences" of Israel's tampering with peace accords.

"The only way to improve ties is that Israel respect all accords signed with Arab parties and start to immediately implement the Oslo accords without amendment or change," Rifai was quoted by the state news agency Petra after meeting Dore.

King Hussein, arriving from London after a private visit, told reporters the Middle East peace process was endangered unless Israeli-Palestinian talks on a long delayed pull-back from the West Bank town of Hebron succeeded.
"Peace was in jeopardy and still is, unless these negotiations lead to concrete and conclusive results...I hope they will," the monarch said.
The king repeated earlier warnings, believed to be the toughest against Israel since the peace treaty, that its policies were pushing the region towards wider Arab-Israeli conflict.
In a belligerent tone that has been absent in recent years officials now say that Israel's hardline policies are driving the region into a wider Arab-Israeli conflict.
"I described the situation as being one in which we were on the brink of abyss...comprehensive peace in the region was in jeopardy and still is," the monarch emphasised.
The monarch, repeated twice but without elaborating, that he expected "to hear some good news soon".
Officials said the king may be referring to an Israeli promise of a more flexible position over its pullback from Hebron in resumed talks in the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Taba this week.

Jordan is seriously questioning Netanyahu's willingness to honour past commitments -- citing failure to redeploy troops from Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns to fall under Palestinian self-rule in line with a 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal.
King Hussein confirmed a visit on Monday by Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to brief him on progress in resumed Israeli-Palestinians talks since a recent flareup in violence.

Asked about the planned visit by Israeli President Ezer Weizman, the monarch was non-committal about its timing, saying:"Under the circumstances I think it might happen rather soon..but I do not know exactly when."
In recent days, King Hussein has stepped up his public support of Arafat while distancing himself from Netanyahu.
The monarch had previously urged wary Arabs to give Netanyahu a chance to show his intentions after his May election. This meant he was far more positive than other Arab leaders towards Netanyahu.

Worried officials say recent violence in Palestinian territories, which has left 75 dead, also raised the fear of chaos on the West Bank that could spill over into the kingdom because of close demographic, political and economic links.
